lesson.title: Distance Never Lies: The Absolute Value Function
lesson.summary: The absolute value function measures distance from a target value, producing a V-shaped graph built from two linear pieces.
lesson.body:
The absolute value of a number measures its distance from zero on the number line, and since distance is never negative, |x| is always zero or positive no matter what x is. Turning that idea into a function, f(x) = |x|, gives every real number input a nonnegative output, which produces a distinctive V-shaped graph instead of a straight line.

You already know from the previous chapter that piecewise functions switch formulas depending on which part of the domain the input falls into, and the absolute value function is one of the simplest possible examples: |x| = x when x >= 0, and |x| = -x when x < 0. The two pieces are both straight lines, one with slope 1 and one with slope -1, and they meet exactly at the origin, which is why the graph looks like a checkmark or the letter V rather than a smooth curve.

Consider the function f(x) = |x - 3|. To evaluate it, first simplify the expression inside the absolute value bars, then take its distance from zero. At x = 1: f(1) = |1 - 3| = |-2| = 2. At x = 3: f(3) = |3 - 3| = |0| = 0. At x = 7: f(7) = |7 - 3| = |4| = 4. Notice that f(1) and f(7) are equal, both 2, even though 1 and 7 are different distances from 0 on the number line; that symmetry happens because 1 and 7 are the same distance, 2 units, from x = 3 in opposite directions, and absolute value only cares about distance, not direction.

That balancing point, x = 3, is called the vertex of the graph, the single point where the two linear pieces meet, and it occurs exactly where the expression inside the bars equals zero. The vertex here is (3, 0), the lowest point on the graph, since every other output is a positive distance away from it. Because inputs on either side of 3 produce identical positive outputs, the graph is a mirror image of itself across the vertical line x = 3. The domain of this function is all real numbers, since you can subtract 3 from anything, but the range is restricted to y >= 0, since absolute value never produces a negative result.

Absolute value functions also connect directly to solving absolute value equations. Setting f(x) = |x - 3| equal to a positive number, like 5, means asking which inputs are exactly 5 units from 3, and the answer is two values, x = 8 and x = -2, since |8 - 3| = |5| = 5 and |-2 - 3| = |-5| = 5. Graphically, this is the same as finding where the horizontal line y = 5 crosses the V-shaped graph, which it does at two points because a horizontal line above the vertex always crosses both branches of the V.

The plain function f(x) = |x|, with its vertex sitting right at the origin, is the simplest version of this entire family of V-shaped graphs, and every other absolute value function, including f(x) = |x - 3|, is really just a shifted copy of it. That idea, that one basic graph can represent an entire family of related functions, is precisely what the next chapter on parent functions is built around.
